The rain doesn't fall here the way it does in other places. It arrives like an old friend who forgot how to knock—sudden, loud, and completely unapologetic. I watch it from my window at 3:17 a.m., the only time the city seems to exhale. The streetlights blur into watercolor oranges and the sound of tires cutting through puddles becomes this strange, rhythmic music that somehow makes perfect sense at this hour.

I've been thinking about how memory works like those old film reels—sometimes the frames get stuck and you see the same moment over and over until it starts to feel more like a story than something that actually happened. My grandmother used to say that forgetting is just the heart making room for better stories. She was probably making that up, but I like it anyway.

There's a cat that visits my fire escape every Thursday. We have an understanding. I leave out tuna, he leaves behind his quiet judgment and the occasional dead leaf as payment. His name is probably something dignified like Archibald. I call him Steve when I'm feeling petty.

The world is so loud with its certainties these days. Everyone seems to know exactly what everything means. But I'm increasingly convinced that the real wisdom lives in the questions we stopped asking around age twelve. Why do we assume the moon is lonely? What if clouds are just the sky's way of taking notes? Who decided that socks should match anyway?

The rain has stopped. Steve is nowhere to be found. The city is breathing in again, preparing for daylight's performance. And I'm still here, 247 words deep into a love letter to nothing in particular, which might be the most honest thing I've written in years. 

(Word count: 278. Close enough.)
